dtz.lead: Trinity College London’s Integrated Skills in English at level B1: Reading & Writing and Speaking & Listening.
dtz.who.title: Who is ISE I for?
dtz.who.badge.course: Pass, Merit or Distinction per skill
dtz.who.text: ISE I is Trinity College London's exam at level B1. It tests all four skills in two modules, Reading & Writing and Speaking & Listening, and people take it for study, work and, in some cases, UK visa applications. Check the current rules for your purpose before you book.
dtz.fmt.ads.what: Match short adverts to the people they suit
dtz.fmt.tf.what: Understand a newspaper article and judge statements about it
dtz.fmt.forum.what: Match statements to people; understand an interview
dtz.fmt.form.what: Transfer information from an e-mail into a form
dtz.fmt.write.what: A personal reply e-mail + a formal letter
dtz.fmt.speak.what: Describe a picture, then answer personal follow-up questions
dtz.fmt.speak.source: Our own classroom material — 90 sec. describing + 90 sec. follow-up questions
dtz.format.note: The task types above are those of our B1 skills mock, which also feeds our interactive reading & writing and speaking exercises. The real ISE I has its own task structure: Reading & Writing takes 2 hours (long reading, multi-text reading, reading into writing, extended writing) and Speaking & Listening about 18 minutes, one-to-one with an examiner. Our ISE I practice set follows that structure.
dtz.scoring.title: How ISE I is marked
dtz.scoring.text: Trinity has no percentage pass mark. Each of the four skills (reading, writing, speaking, listening) gets its own result: Distinction, Merit, Pass or Fail. Reading & Writing and Speaking & Listening are two modules, and you can take them at different times. In our B1 skills mock the point bands are our own guide, not Trinity’s.
dtz.set.title: A B1 skills mock: listening, reading and writing
dtz.set.text: Nine parts, 45 scored tasks: listening parts 1–4 and reading parts 1–5, plus a writing task. At the end you see your result by part, with our own point bands as a guide. Progress stays saved in the browser.
dtz.mock.title: Shorter: mock reading test (tasks 1–4)
dtz.mock.text: All four reading tasks as one continuous test, with an overall result at the end.
dtz.practice.intro: These practice tools train the skills that ISE I tests, at level B1.
telc.lead: Trinity College London’s Integrated Skills in English: ISE Foundation (A2), ISE I (B1) and ISE II (B2), with reading, writing, speaking and listening tested together.
telc.who.title: Who is Trinity ISE for?
telc.who.text: There is one Trinity ISE exam for each level: ISE Foundation (A2), ISE I (B1) and ISE II (B2). Each has two modules, Reading & Writing and Speaking & Listening. People take ISE for study, work and, in some cases, UK visa applications. Check the current rules for your purpose before you book.
telc.sprachbausteine.note: ISE tests the skills together: for example, you read a text and then write about it. Grammar and vocabulary are not a separate paper; they count in how well you read, write, speak and listen.
telc.moreLevels.title: Other levels
telc.moreLevels.text: Times, task counts and marking differ between the ISE levels. For Foundation, I or II, check the official Trinity specification for your level. We enter here only what we can document, rather than estimating figures.

goethe.lead: The exams of Cambridge University Press & Assessment – recognised worldwide by employers, colleges and universities.
goethe.who.title: Who are the Cambridge English exams for?
goethe.who.text: Each Cambridge English exam is aimed at one level: A2 Key, B1 Preliminary, B2 First. Employers, colleges and universities in many countries accept them. The certificates have no expiry date, but some institutions ask for a recent result.
goethe.modell.title: Official sample tests
goethe.moreLevels.text: Cambridge English publishes free sample papers for every exam on its website. The formats above come from Cambridge’s own exam information; we only enter what we can document, rather than estimating figures.
goethe.a1.title: A1: our own practice test
goethe.a1.text: Cambridge has no adult exam below A2 Key. Our A1 English practice test uses simple task types like those in A2 Key, at A1 level. It is not an official exam, and its 60 % pass line is our own convention.

testdaf.lead: The English test many universities ask for. It reports band scores from 0 to 9 and has no pass mark.
testdaf.who.title: Who is IELTS Academic for?
testdaf.who.text: IELTS Academic is aimed mainly at people applying to universities and colleges that teach in English. Everyone sits the same four parts (Listening, Reading, Writing and Speaking). Each skill gets a band score from 0 to 9, and you also get an overall band. There is no pass mark: every institution decides which bands it asks for, so check the requirement of your course.

testdaf.fmt.sprechen.what: A face-to-face interview with an examiner
testdaf.format.note: There is no pass mark: each skill gets a band score from 0 to 9, you get an overall band, and every university or employer decides which bands it asks for. We have no official IELTS material of our own; the details here are general, public information about the test. For the current format and timings, check the official IELTS website.

All texts and tasks are written by us, not official exam material. Listening and Speaking are not included yet.

lid.who.badge.noCefr: No CEFR level — a knowledge test
lid.who.text: The Life in the UK test does not test your level of English but your knowledge of British society, history and traditions. Most people need it to apply for settlement (indefinite leave to remain) or British citizenship.

grammatik.artikel.intro: Every German noun has a gender — and the gender is not in the word itself but in the article in front of it. That is why you never learn „Tisch“, always „der Tisch“.
grammatik.ja-nein-fragen.intro: With no question word, the verb slides right to the front: „Er kommt aus Berlin.“ becomes „Kommt er aus Berlin?“ And a negative question is answered not with ja but with doch.
grammatik.w-fragen.intro: A W-question starts with the question word, and the verb comes right away in position 2. A1: wer, was, wo, wann, wie — and the pattern. A2: wen or wem? welcher or was für ein? mit wem or womit? seit wann, wie lange — and questions in the Perfekt and with modal verbs.
grammatik.praesens.intro: The verb adapts to the person: ich lern-e, du lern-st, er lern-t. The stem stays, only the ending changes — and sein and haben go their own way.
grammatik.verb-position-2.intro: A statement (Aussagesatz) is a main clause (Hauptsatz) that says something. The verb is always in Position 2 — even when the subject is not at the front: „Heute gehe ich ins Kino.“
grammatik.konjugation.intro: Conjugation tables for the most important verbs — present, simple past, present perfect, past perfect and future. To look up and to practise.
grammatik.plural.intro: In the plural the article is always die — but the noun has five ways of becoming more: -e, -er, -(e)n, -s or no ending at all, often with an umlaut.
grammatik.possessivartikel.intro: Whose is it? mein Buch, dein Auto, ihre Tasche. A1: the same endings as ein/eine. A2: in the dative too — mit meinem Bruder, bei meiner Oma, von seinen Eltern.
grammatik.imperativ.intro: Requests, instructions, tips: the imperative puts the verb at the start. A1: Komm! Kommt! Kommen Sie! — with du the pronoun disappears, with Sie it stays. A2: with pronouns (Gib es mir!), reflexive (Setz dich!), together (Gehen wir!) and even more polite as a question (Könnten Sie …?).
grammatik.aduso.intro: These five words join two sentences. They don't change the word order: after them comes a completely normal sentence, and the verb stays in position 2.
grammatik.nomen.intro: A noun is a name: for a person, an animal, a thing, a place or an idea. In German you can spot it at once — it starts with a capital letter and usually has an article in front of it.
grammatik.komposita.intro: In German, nouns are often put together: das Haus + die Tür = die Haustür. The last word decides the article and the plural; the first word says what kind of thing it is.
grammatik.wortarten.intro: Every word has a type. If you know the word class, you know what the word does in the sentence: nouns are written with a capital letter, verbs change with the person — and separable verbs split in the sentence.
grammatik.akkusativ.intro: Nominative → accusative: der → den, die → die, das → das, die (pl.) → die. After haben, brauchen, sehen.
grammatik.dativ.intro: The dative answers the question „wem?“ (to whom?): Ich schenke meiner Mutter Blumen. It follows verbs like helfen, danken and gefallen, and the prepositions aus, bei, mit, nach, seit, von, zu. Masculine and neuter take dem, feminine der, plural den — and the noun gets -n.
grammatik.modalverben.intro: müssen, können, dürfen, sollen, wollen, mögen — they say not what happens but how it is meant: obligation, permission, ability or wish. The second verb moves to the end of the sentence.
grammatik.negation.intro: Two words share the work of negating: „kein“ replaces „ein“ in front of a noun, „nicht“ negates everything else. And „nicht“ almost always sits further right than you expect.
grammatik.perfekt.intro: In conversation, the past is told in the Perfekt. Two questions to settle: which auxiliary verb — and what is the Partizip II?
grammatik.satzstellung.intro: In a German statement the conjugated verb always stands in position 2 — whatever is in position 1. The second part of the verb waits at the end of the sentence: that is the Satzklammer, the sentence bracket.
grammatik.wechselpraepositionen.intro: Nine prepositions can take either dative or accusative. The question decides: „Wo?“ means dative, „Wohin?“ means accusative. Im Kino is not ins Kino.
grammatik.positionsverben.intro: Stellen or stehen? Legen or liegen? The where-to verb takes an object and is regular (Ich stelle die Kiste in den Flur), the where verb takes none and is irregular (Die Kiste steht im Flur). The simple past and perfect of the four pairs come on top.
grammatik.praepositionen.intro: Some verbs need a fixed preposition. Learn the pattern, then practise it in five different task types — like a page from a coursebook.
grammatik.trennbare-verben.intro: With anrufen, aufstehen or einkaufen the verb splits: Ich rufe dich morgen an. The prefix is stressed and goes to the end of the sentence. In the perfect tense, ge goes in the middle: angerufen.
grammatik.zusammengesetzte-verben.intro: With weggehen, losfahren or zurückkommen, the first part already tells you what happens: Der Bus fährt weg. Der Film geht los. Ich komme gleich zurück. It also works without a verb: Der Bus ist weg. Was ist los?
grammatik.als-oder-wenn.intro: In many languages the two are the same word — in German they are not. A single moment in the past is always „als“; anything repeated, conditional or future is „wenn“.
grammatik.n-deklination.intro: A small group of masculine nouns adds -(e)n in every case except the nominative: der Herr, but an Herrn Schneider. Knowing them is what makes a letter come out right.
grammatik.genitiv.intro: The genitive says who something belongs to: das Auto meines Bruders. It also follows wegen, trotz and während. In conversation people often say von + dative — in letters and in the exam, the genitive counts.
grammatik.adjektivdeklination.intro: The adjective's ending depends not on the noun but on what stands in front of it. Three types — definite article, indefinite article, no article — and the pattern is yours.
grammatik.adjektivdeklination-a2.intro: der neue Tisch, ein neuer Tisch: after der/die/das the adjective only has -e or -en. After ein it sometimes steps in with -er or -es. The short version for A2: nominative, accusative, dative – no genitive.
grammatik.ordinalzahlen.intro: First, second, third: this is how you say the date, the floor and the order. Up to 19 you add -te to the number, from 20 on -ste. After am, im and zum it is -ten: am dritten Mai.
grammatik.zahlen.intro: From zero to a thousand: you say the ones first, then the tens, and write it all as one word: einundzwanzig, dreihundertfünfzig.
grammatik.adjektive-nach-sein.intro: After sein, werden and bleiben the adjective has no ending: Die Küche ist klein. Das Wetter wird schön. With nicht, sehr, zu and ganz you can say more.
grammatik.gern.intro: What do you like doing, what not? With gern and nicht gern you say what you enjoy. The word comes after the verb: Ich spiele gern Fußball.
grammatik.praeteritum-sein-haben.intro: War and hatte are the simple past of sein and haben: Wo warst du gestern? Ich hatte keine Zeit. Only with these two verbs do people almost always use the Präteritum instead of the Perfekt in conversation.
grammatik.berufe-mit-in.intro: Der Lehrer, die Lehrerin: for women you add -in, in the plural -innen. With a job you use no ein or eine: Ich bin Lehrerin.
grammatik.konjunktiv2-hoeflich.intro: With hätte, könnte, würde and solltest you sound friendlier: Ich hätte gern einen Kaffee. Könnten Sie mir helfen? An deiner Stelle würde ich zum Arzt gehen.
grammatik.infinitiv-mit-zu.intro: An infinitive clause has no subject of its own — the main clause's subject carries over. The „zu“ sits right at the end before the infinitive, and inside the word with separable verbs.
grammatik.praeteritum-plusquamperfekt.in: Three past tenses, three jobs: Perfekt for conversation, Präteritum for narrating and writing — and Plusquamperfekt for everything that happened before that.
grammatik.indirekte-fragen.intro: „Wo ist der Bahnhof?“ sounds curt. „Können Sie mir sagen, wo der Bahnhof ist?“ sounds polite — and turns the question into a subordinate clause with the verb at the end.
grammatik.passiv.intro: Active → passive with a modal verb: subject + modal + … + Partizip II + werden. "Ich buche das Hotel." → "Das Hotel muss gebucht werden."
grammatik.passiv-b1.intro: Die Straße wird repariert – who does it doesn't matter. The passive is formed with werden and the Partizip II: wird gebaut, wurde gebaut, ist gebaut worden. Watch out: in the Perfekt it's worden, not geworden.
grammatik.wortbildung-nomen.intro: Verbs and adjectives become nouns: wohnen → die Wohnung, frei → die Freiheit. The ending tells you the article and often the plural: -chen is always das, -in and -ung are always die.
grammatik.temporale-praepositionen-b1.in: Exactly when? Innerhalb einer Woche means: at the latest then. Während des Urlaubs and beim Essen mean: at the same time. Add bis zum Wochenende, zwischen 8 und 9 Uhr and über Nacht.
grammatik.infinitiv-ohne-zu.intro: After some verbs the infinitive stands without zu: Ich kann schwimmen. Ich höre ihn singen. Wir gehen einkaufen. After others you need zu: Ich versuche, früher aufzustehen. Here you learn which verbs belong to which group.
grammatik.funktionen-von-werden.intro: The little verb werden has five jobs: Es wird kalt. Ich werde anrufen. Er wird wohl krank sein. Das Auto wird repariert. Ich würde gern kommen. You can tell the job from what stands with werden.
grammatik.konjunktiv2.intro: With the subjunctive II you talk about wishes and conditions that are not real: Wenn ich Zeit hätte, würde ich kommen. You also need it for polite requests and advice: Könnten Sie mir helfen? For the past you use hätte or wäre + past participle.
grammatik.relativpronomen.intro: A relative clause describes a noun more precisely: die Nachbarin, die mir hilft. The relative pronoun takes its gender and number from the noun before it — but its case from its role in the relative clause. The verb goes at the end.
grammatik.irgend.intro: You don't know exactly, or it doesn't matter: just stick „irgend“ in front of a question word, the indefinite article or „welche“ — and the statement is comfortably vague.
grammatik.fokuspartikeln.intro: „Auch ich schenke dir Blumen“ and „Ich schenke dir auch Blumen“ say two different things. Focus particles sit directly in front of the part they highlight — and that changes the meaning.
grammatik.negationswoerter.intro: Beyond nicht and kein there is a whole system: nichts, niemand, nirgendwo, noch nie, nicht mehr — plus the affixes un-, in- and -los, which negate a word from the inside.
grammatik.nomen-verb-verbindungen.intro: „Rücksicht nehmen“, „in Frage kommen“, „zur Verfügung stehen“ — fixed noun-plus-verb pairs in which the verb has almost no meaning of its own left. They have to be learnt whole.
grammatik.partizip-als-adjektiv.intro: A whole sentence becomes one word: „Der Zug fährt ein“ → „der einfahrende Zug“. Partizip I means: happening right now. Partizip II means: finished, or done to it.
grammatik.adjektive-als-nomen.intro: Adjectives become nouns: der Bekannte, die Jugendliche, etwas Neues. They are capitalised and take the ending of an adjective – for people after the article, for things after etwas, nichts, viel, wenig and alles.
grammatik.zweiteilige-konnektoren.intro: These connectors always come in pairs: „nicht nur … sondern auch“, „weder … noch“, „je … desto“. Once you use the first half, you owe the second.
grammatik.konditionalsaetze.intro: With wenn you state the normal condition; falls is more cautious: only in case. Sofern and vorausgesetzt name a requirement, es sei denn the exception. The word also decides where the verb goes.
grammatik.konsekutivsaetze.intro: With sodass and so … dass you state the result in a subordinate clause, with the verb at the end. Folglich and infolgedessen start a new main clause: the verb comes right after them. With a noun you say infolge + genitive.
grammatik.zumal-wohingegen.intro: With zumal you add a second, stronger reason. Wohingegen and während show a contrast, and insofern … als limits a statement. All three send the verb to the end of the clause.
grammatik.modalsaetze.intro: With indem and dadurch, dass you say how or by what means something is achieved. With ohne dass you say what is missing. The verb is always at the end. With ohne and (an)statt the subject decides: same subject → … zu, different subject → dass.
grammatik.reflexive-verben.intro: With reflexive verbs, the pronoun means the same person as the subject: Ich wasche mich. If there is also an accusative object, the pronoun is in the dative: Ich wasche mir die Hände.
grammatik.nebensaetze-weil-dass.intro: After weil, dass and wenn, the conjugated verb goes to the end of the sentence: …, weil ich krank bin. If the sentence starts with the subordinate clause, two verbs stand in the middle: Wenn ich Zeit habe, komme ich.
grammatik.komparativ-superlativ.intro: With the comparative you compare two things: Der Bus ist billiger als das Taxi. With the superlative you say who or what is number one: Das Fahrrad ist am billigsten. If two things are the same, you say so … wie.
grammatik.lokale-praepositionen.intro: Where from? Where to? Where? The question decides: aus der Türkei, nach Berlin, zum Arzt, beim Arzt, nach Hause, zu Hause. You need these little words every day.
grammatik.positionsadverbien.intro: Where is something? Das Büro ist oben. Where are you going? Ich gehe nach oben. Then there are hin and her: Komm her! Geh hin! With these small words you say exactly where something is and where it goes.
grammatik.personalpronomen.intro: Pronouns stand for people and things: ich, du, er, sie … A1: mich, dich, ihn (accusative) and mir, dir, ihm (dative). A2: two pronouns in one sentence — Kannst du es mir geben? —, pronouns after prepositions, and set phrases like Mir ist kalt.
grammatik.indefinitpronomen.intro: For people: man (people in general), jemand (someone), niemand (nobody). For things: etwas (something), nichts (nothing). Ist jemand da? – Nein, niemand. Brauchst du etwas? – Nein, nichts.
grammatik.temporale-praepositionen.intro: When? um 8 Uhr, am Montag, im Mai. With von … bis you give the start and the end. Seit means: it started earlier and is still going on now.
grammatik.futur.intro: With werden + infinitive you talk about the future: Ich werde Sie morgen anrufen. In everyday speech the present tense with a time phrase is often enough. With wohl, the future becomes a guess: Er wird wohl krank sein.
grammatik.temporale-nebensaetze.intro: With bevor, nachdem, während, seit and bis you say when something happens: before, after, at the same time, or up to a point in time. The verb goes to the end. After nachdem the tense changes.
grammatik.da-wo-woerter.intro: For things you say darauf, damit, daran — for people auf ihn, mit ihr. Questions work the same way: worauf? for things, auf wen? for people.
grammatik.lassen.intro: With lassen you say that someone else does something for you: Ich lasse das Auto reparieren. Or that someone is allowed to do something: Die Eltern lassen das Kind spielen. After it comes the infinitive without zu.
grammatik.modalpartikeln.intro: Little words like doch, mal, ja, eben and halt don't change the content, they change the tone: a request sounds friendlier, a question more interested. They are spoken unstressed and sit in the middle of the sentence.
grammatik.adjektive-mit-praepositionen.i: Many adjectives have a fixed preposition: stolz auf, zufrieden mit, abhängig von. The preposition decides the case. After darauf, damit … a dass-clause or a zu-infinitive can follow.
grammatik.konnektoren-grund-gegengrund.i: With weil, da and denn you give a reason, with deshalb the result. Obwohl and trotzdem say: something happens, but not the way you would expect. The word also decides where the verb goes.
grammatik.finalsaetze.intro: With um … zu and damit you say what you do something for. The key question is: who acts in the goal? If it is the same person, um … zu works. If it is a different person, only damit works.
grammatik.zustandspassiv.intro: Die Heizung wird repariert — the technician is still working. Die Heizung ist repariert — the work is done. With werden, the passive describes a process; with sein, a state.
grammatik.relativsaetze-was-wo.intro: Not every relative clause starts with der, die or das. After alles, nichts or das Beste comes was, after places often wo — and wer talks about anyone the statement applies to: Wer zu spät kommt, muss warten.
grammatik.konjunktiv-1.intro: With the subjunctive I you report what other people have said: Die Ministerin sagte, sie habe keine Zeit. You find it mainly in the news and in reports. If the form is the same as the indicative, you use the subjunctive II instead.
grammatik.subjektive-modalverben.intro: Modal verbs don't only say what someone must or wants to do. They also show how sure the speaker is, or where they heard something: Sie muss es gewusst haben. Er soll reich sein. For the past you use the perfect infinitive: gewusst haben, gewesen sein.
grammatik.passiversatz.intro: Das Problem lässt sich lösen. Das Problem ist lösbar. Das Problem ist zu lösen. This is how you say the passive with können or müssen more briefly — typical of newspapers, official letters and science.
grammatik.partizipialattribute.intro: A whole relative clause fits between the article and the noun: der seit Jahren leer stehende Laden. Participle I means active and happening at the same time, participle II means passive or completed, zu + participle I means: this has to be done.
grammatik.nominalisierung.intro: In the nominal style, verbs become nouns and subordinate clauses become prepositional phrases: weil die Preise steigen → wegen der steigenden Preise. This is how reports, applications and academic texts are written. At C1 you need both directions.
grammatik.nominale-praepositionen.intro: Reports, letters from the authorities and specialist texts use prepositions like aufgrund, angesichts or mangels. Almost all of them take the genitive. There are two exceptions you need to know: zufolge comes after the noun and takes the dative, and with dank both are possible.
grammatik.irreale-vergleiche.intro: With als ob, als wenn or als you compare something with a situation that isn't true: Er tut, als wäre er der Chef. The verb is in subjunctive II — at the end after als ob, straight after als.
grammatik.futur-2.intro: The future perfect guesses what has already happened: Er wird den Zug verpasst haben. Or it says what will be finished by a certain time: Bis Freitag werde ich den Bericht geschrieben haben. In conversation people often use the perfect tense instead.
grammatik.es-korrelat.intro: Often „es“ stands in a sentence without meaning anything. Sometimes it only holds position 1, sometimes it announces a dass-clause, sometimes it belongs to the verb for good. If you know when it drops out, you write with more confidence.
grammatik.textkohaerenz.intro: A good text holds together: reference words pick up what is already known, adverbs link sentences, and signposting phrases show the thread. If you use them on purpose, your writing in telc and Goethe C1 is more convincing.
grammatik.verbpraefixe.intro: Die Fähre setzt uns über — sie übersetzt den Text. With durch-, über-, um-, unter-, wieder- and voll-, stress decides: if the prefix is stressed, the verb is separable. If the verb stem is stressed, it stays together.
grammatik.nutzen-benutzen.intro: Many verbs exist with and without a prefix (Präfix): nutzen and benutzen, antworten and beantworten, kommen and bekommen. Sometimes one verb is a part of the other, sometimes they overlap, and sometimes they have nothing to do with each other.
grammatik.verben-als-nomen.intro: You can make a noun out of almost any verb: wandern → das Wandern, die Wanderung, der Wanderer. The ending often already shows the article. And das Wandern is not the same as die Wanderung.
grammatik.artikel-oder-nicht.intro: „Ich würde im Restaurant gerne Fisch essen.“ Why is there no article here? der means: we already know it. ein means: new, one of many. Without an article you speak in general, for example about food, jobs or languages.
grammatik.welcher-dieser.intro: Welchen Mantel nimmst du? – Diesen. welcher (which) and dieser (this) have the endings of der, die, das: welcher, welche, welches – in the accusative welchen, in the dative welchem and welcher. Also: dieser on its own as a pronoun, welcher or was für ein, and jeder.
grammatik.artikel-oder-nicht.brief:

kultur.duzen-siezen.cardIntro: English has only one word for you.
kultur.pfand.cardIntro: In the UK, people queue for buses, shops and many other things.
kultur.sonntagsruhe.cardIntro: On Sundays, many shops in the UK open for fewer hours.
kultur.trinkgeld.cardIntro: In a UK restaurant, a tip of about 10 to 12.5% is normal.
kultur.bundeslaender.cardIntro: The UK is made up of four nations: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.
kultur.feiertage.cardIntro: A bank holiday is a public holiday: many people do not work, and banks and offices close.
kultur.muelltrennung.cardIntro: In the UK, your local council collects rubbish and recycling from your home.
kultur.termine.cardIntro: In the UK, you usually book an appointment before you see a doctor, a dentist or a hairdresser.
kultur.anmeldung.cardIntro: There is no residence registration in the UK, so you do not have to report your address to the city.
kultur.krankenversicherung.cardIntro: The NHS (National Health Service) gives most health care free at the point of use.
kultur.mieten.cardIntro: When you rent a flat in the UK, the monthly rent is only part of the cost.
kultur.schulsystem.cardIntro: In England children go to primary school and then secondary school, and they stay in education or training until they are 18.
kultur.ausbildung.cardIntro: After school, young people in the UK can either go to university or train in a job as an apprentice.
kultur.kuendigung.cardIntro: When you leave a job in the UK, or an employer ends your contract, a period of notice usually applies.
The BBC is the UK's public broadcaster, and it is paid for mainly by a licence fee rather than by adverts.
kultur.vereine.cardIntro: Much of social life in the UK happens in clubs, societies and volunteering groups, which are usually informal and easy to join.
kultur.foederalismus.cardIntro: Ask who runs education in the UK and the honest answer is: it depends where you are.
kultur.sozialversicherung.cardIntro: National Insurance sounds like an insurance scheme, but in practice it works largely as a tax that also builds your entitlement to certain benefits.
kultur.wahlen.cardIntro: In a UK general election you cast a single vote for one candidate in your local constituency, and you do not vote for the Prime Minister at all.
kultur.erinnerungskultur.cardIntro: Every November, much of the UK pauses to remember those who died in war.
kultur.grundgesetz.cardIntro: The United Kingdom has no single written document called 'the Constitution'.
kultur.mitbestimmung.cardIntro: In the UK, workers' rights come mainly from legislation and from individual employment contracts, with trade unions acting as a collective voice for those who choose to join.

wissen.rights.p2: What is deliberately NOT here: audio and book files from publishers and exam boards (coursebooks, Cambridge, IELTS or Trinity practice books). We are not allowed to pass those on, not even for free and not even in class. Instead, we link to the official sample papers where they are published — see “Official materials”.

Stage 1 is a one-minute long turn about a photo, as in Part 2 of the Cambridge B1 Preliminary and B2 First speaking tests. Stage 2 is a talk from a topic card: one minute to make notes, then up to two minutes of speaking, as in IELTS Speaking Part 2. ap.ex.vowel: “{word}” starts with a vowel sound, so it takes “an”: an {word}.
ap.ex.consonant: “{word}” starts with a consonant sound, so it takes “a”: a {word}.
ap.ex.yu: “{word}” starts with a vowel letter but a consonant sound (like “you” or “w”), so it takes “a”: a {word}.
ap.ex.silent: “{word}” starts with a consonant letter but a vowel sound (a silent h, or a letter said like “em” or “ex”), so it takes “an”: an {word}.
ap.ex.some: “{word}” is uncountable: in English you don't count it. So you say “some {word}”, not “a {word}”.
ap.ex.plural: “{word}” is always plural, so you say “some {word}”, not “a {word}”.
ap.ex.vowel.leicht: The word starts with the sound a, e, i, o or u. Then you say “an”: an {word}.
ap.ex.consonant.leicht: The word does not start with the sound a, e, i, o or u. Then you say “a”: a {word}.
ap.ex.yu.leicht: Listen to the first sound. It sounds like “you” or “w”. So you say “a”: a {word}.
ap.ex.silent.leicht: Listen to the first sound. You don't say the first letter like “h”. The word starts with a vowel sound. So you say “an”: an {word}.
ap.ex.some.leicht: You can't count {word}. So you say “some {word}”.
ap.ex.plural.leicht: “{word}” is always more than one. So you say “some {word}”.

“From class” – from a real class discussion.
“Facts” – publicly checkable facts about rules, institutions and procedures in the UK (laws, amounts, who is responsible). Written by icanspeak Spanish, not taken from a lesson.

sprechen.check.a1-sich-vorstellen.1: Full sentences, not a list: “I'm 29 years old.”, not just “29”. A job needs a or an: “I'm an electrician.”
sprechen.check.a1-sich-vorstellen.2: End with your free time: the examiner often asks the next question about it.
sprechen.check.a1-bild-bahnhof.0: “I can see …” is the easiest way to start, and it is always right.
sprechen.check.a1-bild-bahnhof.1: “I think …” and “maybe …” let you guess without being sure.
sprechen.check.a1-bild-bahnhof.2: The last sentence is about you: that is what the examiner asks next.
sprechen.check.a1-bild-kueche.0: First count (“two people”), then say the place, then the action. This order always works.
sprechen.check.a1-bild-kueche.1: For what is happening now, use is + -ing: is cooking, is sitting, is watching.
sprechen.check.a1-bild-supermarkt.0: Food words in the plural: apples, bananas, vegetables. But some fruit, some bread: no plural.
sprechen.check.a1-bild-supermarkt.1: “at the checkout”, “by card”, “in cash”: learn the little word with the phrase.
sprechen.check.a1-bild-supermarkt.2: A time phrase at the end (“on Saturday”, “once a week”) sounds practised straight away.
sprechen.check.a1-bild-spielplatz.0: Two people, two sentences: first the boy, then the woman.
sprechen.check.a1-bild-spielplatz.1: One sentence about the weather: the examiner almost always asks.
sprechen.check.a1-bild-spielplatz.2: “because” joins your reason to your sentence: I like the park because it's quiet.
sprechen.check.a2-bild-nachbarschaftsfes: Say what is in the foreground and in the background: that is the step from A1 to A2.
A guess with a reason: “I think it's …, because …”
End with a comparison with your own life or country. At A2 the examiner almost always asks.
sprechen.check.a2-bild-wartezimmer.0: Say how someone feels and why: “She looks worried. Maybe …” Pictures with people almost always get this question.
sprechen.check.a2-bild-wartezimmer.1: Say what you can and can't see: “We can only see the doctor's arm.”
sprechen.check.a2-bild-wartezimmer.2: A real detail from your own life (“two or three weeks”) is worth more than a general sentence.
sprechen.check.b1-bild-bewerbungsgesprae: Use place words to organise what you say: on the left, on the right, opposite, in the background.
Show that a guess is a guess (“I'd guess that …”, “might be”) and give a reason.
The part in the past (“When I applied …, I was …”) is expected at B1, not optional.
One sentence with “In my opinion”: giving your opinion is the real B1 part.
sprechen.check.b1-bild-werkstatt.0: “I suppose …, because …” joins a guess and a reason in one sentence.
sprechen.check.b1-bild-werkstatt.1: Explain a word (apprenticeship, trade) instead of just saying it.
sprechen.check.b1-bild-werkstatt.2: The “why” question gets a real answer with “because” or “One reason could be that …”.
sprechen.check.b1-bild-buergeramt.0: Show how you know something: “You can tell that …, because …”
sprechen.check.b1-bild-buergeramt.1: Give a real example from your own life instead of a general complaint.
sprechen.check.b1-bild-buergeramt.2: “Now I …” shows how things have changed: examiners like to hear that at B1.
You react to the other person instead of working through your own list.
Disagree politely at least once: that is what the task tests.
At the end you clearly agree on every point.
Polite forms with would and could: I'd suggest, I'd go for, could we …?
sprechen.check.b2-bild-wochenmarkt.0: The description is short. At B2 it is the way in, not the task.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-wochenmarkt.1: Both sides are there, with the linking words for them: one clear advantage, on the other hand, we shouldn't forget.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-wochenmarkt.2: Saying “not only …, it's also …” shows you have really thought the question through.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-wochenmarkt.3: The personal ending is honest rather than perfect: that is harder to say and sounds more mature.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-videokonferenz.0: Something you notice in the picture supports your argument (“What strikes me is that …”), not just general knowledge.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-videokonferenz.1: The objection to your own view is there (“Some people might argue …”) and you answer it.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-videokonferenz.2: The difference between “fixed office days for the team” and “a rule for every person” is a fine distinction. That is exactly what separates B2 from B1.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-baustelle-innenst: A detail from the picture (the flats right next to the site) becomes part of the argument, not just a description.
“The real question is not whether …, but how …” moves the discussion on: a strong B2 phrase.
The opinion ends with conditions, not a simple yes or no. That is more balanced and easier to defend.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-wertstoffhof.0: A system is explained, not just judged.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-wertstoffhof.1: The counter-argument and your answer to it are both there.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-wertstoffhof.2: “Recycling limits the damage; it doesn't solve the problem”: a short, sharp sentence at the end stays with the listener.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-wertstoffhof.3: The comparison with your own country doesn't judge; it describes a difference.
schreiben.check.a1-formular-anmeldung.0: Surname and first name are not swapped. Your surname is your family name.
schreiben.check.a1-formular-anmeldung.1: The date is in British order, day/month/year: 04/03/1996. 03/04/1996 would be 3 April.
schreiben.check.a1-formular-anmeldung.2: Town and postcode go in separate fields, even if they are together in the text.
schreiben.check.a1-nachricht-absage.0: All four points are there – in an exam, a missing point costs more than a small grammar mistake.
schreiben.check.a1-nachricht-absage.1: There is a greeting and a sign-off (Hi Mira / Love, Sam).
schreiben.check.a1-nachricht-absage.2: The sentences are short. At A1, “I have to work.” is better than a long sentence with a mistake.
schreiben.check.a2-email-nachbarn.0: The requests are questions (“Could you …?”, “Would you mind …ing?”), not orders (“Water my plants.”, “You must …”).
schreiben.check.a2-email-nachbarn.1: After “Would you mind” comes the -ing form: “Would you mind taking in my post?”, not “Would you mind to take …”.
schreiben.check.a2-email-nachbarn.2: Greeting and sign-off match: Dear Mrs Clarke → Kind regards. “Love” is too familiar for a neighbour you hardly know.
schreiben.check.a2-formular-arztpraxis.0: Numbers are spoken, not written: “the twentieth of November, nineteen eighty-eight” → 20/11/1988, and “oh” in a phone number is the number 0.
schreiben.check.a2-formular-arztpraxis.1: “First appointment?” is never asked in those words – you have to work it out from “No, I only registered with you last week.”
schreiben.check.a2-formular-arztpraxis.2: “That's fine” means the appointment is confirmed, so fill in the doctor, the date and the time. “Half past three” in the afternoon is 3.30 pm (or 15:30).
schreiben.check.b2-beschwerde-reiseveran: No angry words: “I regret to say that there were several serious problems” instead of “this was a disgrace”. At B2 the tone is part of the mark – firm, but never rude.
Each problem is set against a promise (“Your brochure clearly stated … In fact, however, …”). A complaint without that comparison is only an opinion.
There is a clear demand AND a deadline. Without a date, a letter of complaint is not complete.
B2 linking words: since, in addition, however, therefore. Dear Sir or Madam → Yours faithfully (with a name: Dear Ms Jones → Yours sincerely).
schreiben.check.b1-formular-vhs.0: Every field is filled in. An empty field counts as a mistake, even if the information is in the text.
schreiben.check.b1-formular-vhs.1: Copy names, numbers and dates exactly as they are in the text; a date in British order is day, then month (12 August, 12/08).
schreiben.check.b1-formular-vhs.2: Nothing made up: if something is not in the text, leave the field empty or put a dash.
schreiben.check.b1-brief-david.0: Every point in the task is covered. A missing point costs more than three grammar mistakes.
schreiben.check.b1-brief-david.1: Greeting and sign-off suit each other and the person (Hi David … Best wishes / See you soon).
schreiben.check.b1-brief-david.2: The sentences are linked (so, because, but, also, although), not just one after the other.
schreiben.check.b1-fehlerjagd.0: Read first, then compare: discuss the text only once you have marked every mistake you can find.
schreiben.check.b1-fehlerjagd.1: Write down the mistakes you make yourself, too. That is the point of the task.

ac.find.final: In “{word}” the last sound got lost. Say the ending so it can be heard.
ac.find.auslaut: “{word}” ends in a voiced sound. Keep your voice on at the end: bag is not back, prize is not price.
ac.find.keinE: “{word}” ends in a consonant. Stop on it: don't add an “e” or “a”.
ac.find.cluster: In “{word}” consonants come straight after each other. No vowel between them.
ac.find.spst: “{word}” starts with s + consonant. Start with the s straight away, with no vowel before it.
ac.find.verb: In “{word}” the ending was missing. The ending shows who and when: he works, she lived.
ac.find.h: “{word}” starts with h. Breathe it out softly, as if you were breathing on a cold window.
ac.find.rl: In “{word}” listen carefully to r and l: for l your tongue touches behind your top teeth, for r it touches nothing.
ac.find.kurzlang: In “{word}” listen to the vowel: short i (ship) or long ee (sheep)? The length changes the word.
ac.find.pb: “{word}” has p or b: p comes with a small puff of air.
ac.find.eiou: In “{word}” listen to the vowel: e is not i, o is not u.
ac.find.wb: “{word}”: for v your top teeth touch your bottom lip, for b both lips close.
ac.find.betonung: “{word}”: one syllable is strong, the others are weak. Listen again for the strong one.
ac.find.s: “{word}” has a buzzing z sound. Use your voice, like a bee.
ac.find.th: “{word}” has th: the tip of your tongue between your teeth. Not s, t, f, d or z.
ac.find.wv: “{word}”: for w round your lips, as for “oo”; for v your top teeth touch your bottom lip.
ac.find.ae: “{word}” has the a of “cat”: open your mouth wide, tongue low and forward.

mhelp.aria: Help: what is this page for?
mhelp.kultur.what: Here you learn how everyday life in Germany works: bottle deposits, rubbish, public holidays, appointments and much more.
mhelp.kultur.s1: Pick a topic at your level (A1, A2 …).
mhelp.kultur.s2: Read the short text and look at the examples.
mhelp.kultur.s3: Then answer the quiz questions. That way you remember what matters.
mhelp.wortgeschichte.what: Etymology is the story of a word: where it comes from, how it used to sound and what it used to mean. Many German words are very old and related to words in other languages – maybe in yours too.
mhelp.wortgeschichte.s1: “Die Wurzel” (the root) shows the oldest form of the word we know.
mhelp.wortgeschichte.s2: Read the family tree from the bottom up: from the root to the words of today.
mhelp.wortgeschichte.s3: “Spurensuche” shows the word in your language. Tip: tap the speaker to hear the word.
mhelp.grammatik.what: Every grammar topic, sorted by level — each with a rule and exercises.
mhelp.grammatik.s1: Choose your level and a topic — or „Lieber geführt?“ to go step by step in the right order.
mhelp.grammatik.s2: Read the rule first, then do the exercises.
mhelp.grammatik.s3: Your results are saved. You can see them under „Mein Fortschritt“.
mhelp.hoeren.what: Practise listening: announcements, phone calls, conversations and radio pieces from A1 to B2.
mhelp.hoeren.s1: Choose a text at your level.
mhelp.hoeren.s2: Listen as often as you like — slower, too.
mhelp.hoeren.s3: Answer the questions. Afterwards the transcript helps you.
mhelp.lesen.what: Practise reading with real kinds of text: signs, adverts, emails and articles.
mhelp.lesen.s1: Choose a task at your level.
mhelp.lesen.s2: Read the text calmly. There is no rush.
mhelp.lesen.s3: Answer the questions and read the explanation for each answer.
mhelp.sprechen.what: Practise speaking as in the exam: describe pictures, introduce yourself, plan together, discuss.
mhelp.sprechen.s2: Start the timer and speak out loud. The useful phrases help you.
mhelp.sprechen.s3: Afterwards, compare with the model answer.
mhelp.uebungen.what: Your overview: all exercises and your progress in one place.
mhelp.uebungen.s1: At the top you see where you are right now.
mhelp.uebungen.s2: Choose an area: grammar, vocabulary, listening, reading or speaking.
mhelp.uebungen.s3: „Weiter üben“ takes you straight to the next task.
mhelp.aussprache.what: Train your pronunciation: listen to words and sentences, repeat them and record yourself.
mhelp.aussprache.s2: Listen to the word and say it after the speaker.
mhelp.aussprache.s3: Record yourself and compare with the original.
mhelp.wortschatz.what: Learn words with flashcards — with a picture, a German explanation or in your language.
mhelp.wortschatz.s2: Tap the card to flip it, swipe to move on.
mhelp.wortschatz.s3: At the top you choose: „Auf Deutsch“, your language, or „Alle Sprachen“ for the whole class.

nsw.why.title: Why look things up?
nsw.why.p1: Nobody learns every form by heart – native speakers look things up too. If you know where the answer is, you write with more confidence and don't have to guess.
nsw.why.p2: And the best part: every time you look something up, it sticks a little better. You learn along the way.

nsw.what.title: What is a reference?
nsw.what.p: You don't read a reference from cover to cover. You open it when you have a question – and find the answer in seconds: as a table, with a rule and an example sentence.
nsw.ueben.title: Practise
nsw.ueben.p: You learn a topic step by step: rule, exercises, feedback.
nsw.nach.title: Look it up
nsw.nach.p: You have a specific question – during homework, in an email, just before the exam. Look it up, keep writing.
nsw.tips.title: How it helps you
nsw.tip1.p: Not sure about a form? Look it up instead of guessing.
nsw.tip2.p: A word like “went” or “broken”? The verb tables give you the base form.
nsw.tip3.p: Irregular verbs and verbs with prepositions come up in many exams. Going through the lists once is worth it.
nsw.tip4.p: Every page can be printed, shared and played as a live quiz with the whole class.

sprachen.title: English around the world
sprachen.lead: Where English is spoken, which languages it is related to – and how close your first language is to English.
sprachen.stat.native: people speak English as their first language
sprachen.stat.second: speak it as a second or foreign language
sprachen.stat.official: countries with English as an official language
sprachen.stat.eu: the language with the most speakers in the world
sprachen.map.title: Where English is spoken
sprachen.map.lead: Tap a country or a dot. The colours show how English is used there.
sprachen.map.empty: Pick a country on the map – or in the list below.
sprachen.count.native: people have English as their first language
sprachen.count.minority: people speak only English at home
sprachen.count.dialect: people can hold a conversation in English
sprachen.count.note: Rounded figures from censuses: USA 2022, Australia 2021, India 2011.
sprachen.c.GBR: About 69 million people live in the UK, and almost all of them speak English. Welsh is also an official language in Wales, and Scottish Gaelic, Scots, Irish, Ulster Scots and Cornish are protected minority languages.
sprachen.c.IRL: Irish (Gaelic) is the national and first official language; English is the second official language. In everyday life almost everybody speaks English, and Irish English has its own words, like grand (fine) and craic (fun).
sprachen.c.USA: More people speak English as their first language here than in any other country. About three in four people speak only English at home; Spanish is the second most common language. Congress never passed a law on an official language, but a presidential order in 2025 named English.
sprachen.c.CAN: Canada has two official languages, English and French. English is the first language of more than half of Canadians; French is the main language in Quebec. Canadian spelling mixes British and American: colour, but tire.
sprachen.c.AUS: No law names an official language, but English is the national language. About 72% of people speak only English at home (2021 census). Australians like to shorten words: arvo (afternoon), brekkie (breakfast).
sprachen.c.NZL: New Zealand has three official languages: English, Māori and New Zealand Sign Language. English was used everywhere long before a law made it official in 2026. Many Māori words are part of everyday English here, like kia ora (hello).
sprachen.c.IND: English is an official language of India’s central government, next to Hindi. In the 2011 census about 129 million people said they speak English – very few as their first language. Indian English has its own words, like prepone (to move something to an earlier time).
sprachen.c.PAK: Urdu is the national language. Urdu and English are both official, and English is used in government, the courts, universities and much of business.
sprachen.c.PHL: Filipino and English are the official languages. English is used in schools, government and business, and many people mix the two in everyday talk – often called Taglish.
sprachen.c.SGP: Singapore has four official languages: English, Malay, Mandarin Chinese and Tamil. English is the language of work and school, and in the 2020 census it was the language most families used at home. Singlish, the local everyday English, adds words like lah.
sprachen.c.HKG: A British colony until 1997. Chinese and English are both official. Most people speak Cantonese, and a little over half of the population also speaks English.
sprachen.c.MLT: Maltese and English are the official languages, and laws are written in both. Almost nine in ten people say they can hold a conversation in English, and many students come here to learn it.
sprachen.c.NGA: Nigeria has more than 500 languages. English is the official language of government and schools, and Nigerian Pidgin, an English-based language, connects people all over the country.
sprachen.c.GHA: English is the official language, used in government and schools. Ghana has dozens of local languages; Akan (Twi) is the most widely spoken.
sprachen.c.SLE: English is the official language. In everyday life many people use Krio, an English-based creole, to talk across language groups.
sprachen.c.LBR: From 1822, freed and free-born African Americans settled here, and their English became the language of the state. Today English is the official language, and more than 20 local languages are spoken too.
sprachen.c.CMR: Cameroon has two official languages, French and English. English is mainly used in the Northwest and Southwest regions, where many people also speak Cameroonian Pidgin English.
sprachen.c.KEN: Swahili and English are the official languages; Swahili is also the national language. English is used in schools, the courts and business, while Swahili is spoken more widely in everyday life.
sprachen.c.UGA: English is the official language, used in schools, business and the courts. Swahili became the second official language in 2005, and Luganda is widely spoken around Kampala.
sprachen.c.TZA: Swahili is the main language of the country. English is used next to it as a working language, for example in secondary schools, universities and business.
sprachen.c.RWA: Rwanda has four official languages: Kinyarwanda, English, French and Swahili. Almost everyone speaks Kinyarwanda. In 2008 the government made English the language of schools and of government work instead of French.
sprachen.c.ZMB: English is the official language, used in government and schools. Bemba and Nyanja are widely spoken local languages.
sprachen.c.ZWE: Since its 2013 constitution, Zimbabwe has 16 official languages, including English. Shona and Ndebele are the most widely spoken; English is the main language of government, business and schools.
sprachen.c.BWA: English is the official language. Setswana is the national language, and most people speak it at home.
sprachen.c.NAM: When Namibia became independent in 1990, it chose English as its only official language, although few people spoke it at home. Oshiwambo is the most common home language; Afrikaans and German are spoken too.
sprachen.c.ZAF: South Africa has twelve official languages, including South African Sign Language. English is the home language of fewer than one in ten people, but it is a main language of business, politics and the media.
sprachen.c.PNG: Papua New Guinea has more than 800 languages – more than any other country. English is an official language, used in government, the courts and schools; Tok Pisin, an English-based creole, is the everyday common language.
sprachen.c.FJI: English, Fijian (iTaukei) and Fiji Hindi are the main languages. English was the only official language until 1997 and is still the common language of government, business and education.
sprachen.c.JAM: English is the official language, used in schools, government and the news. In everyday life most people speak Jamaican Patois (Patwa), an English-based creole with many words from African languages.
sprachen.c.TTO: English is the official language. In everyday life people speak Trinidadian or Tobagonian Creole, which are based on English.
sprachen.c.BHS: English is the official language. Many Bahamians also speak Bahamian Creole, which is based on English.
sprachen.c.BRB: English is the official language. Bajan, the local English-based creole, is spoken in everyday life.
sprachen.c.GUY: Guyana is the only country in mainland South America with English as its official language. Most people grow up speaking Guyanese Creole (Creolese), which is based on English.
sprachen.c.BLZ: Belize is the only country in Central America with English as its official language. Belizean Kriol, Spanish and Mayan languages are widely spoken too.
sprachen.c.NLD: English is not official, but about nine in ten Dutch people can hold a conversation in it. Children learn it at school, and many university courses are taught in English.
sprachen.c.DNK: English is not official, but most Danes speak it well. Children start English early at school, and films and series from abroad are usually subtitled, not dubbed.
sprachen.c.SWE: English is not official, but most Swedes speak it well – it is taught from primary school, and English films and series are subtitled, not dubbed.
sprachen.c.MYS: Malay is the official and national language. English was official too until 1967 and is still widely used in business, higher education and the cities.
sprachen.m.gibraltar: A British Overseas Territory at the southern tip of Spain. English is the official language; most Gibraltarians also speak Spanish and Llanito, a local mix of Andalusian Spanish and English.
sprachen.m.bermuda: A British Overseas Territory in the North Atlantic. English is the official language; some families also speak Portuguese – their families came from the Azores.
sprachen.m.falklands: A British Overseas Territory in the South Atlantic, with about 3,700 people (2021 census). English is the official language.
sprachen.benrath.text: In Europe, English is the main language of the UK and Ireland, and an official language in Malta and Gibraltar. In the Netherlands and Scandinavia it is not official, but most people speak it well.
sprachen.tree.title: The language family
sprachen.tree.lead: English is a Germanic language and belongs to the large Indo-European family. Many languages from Iceland to India share the same roots.
sprachen.tree.otherLead: These languages are not related to English. That doesn't make English harder – it just means you learn words fresh instead of recognising them.
sprachen.tree.names: Language names are given in English.
sprachen.cmp.title: How close is your language?
sprachen.cmp.lead: Pick your first language. Eight basic words show how much you already bring with you.
sprachen.cmp.fehler: Typical mistakes with this first language
sprachen.cmp.persisch: Surprise: Persian is related to English! Both are Indo-European. Compare barādar – brother, mādar – mother, nām – name.
sprachen.cmp.russisch: Russian is Slavic – another branch of the same family: брат – brother, три – three, вода – water. Russian nouns have six cases; English nouns have none, and only pronouns change (I – me, she – her).
sprachen.cmp.ukrainisch: Ukrainian is Slavic and distantly related to English: брат – brother, ніч – night, вода – water. Ukrainian nouns have seven cases; in English, word order does that job.
sprachen.cmp.polnisch: Polish is Slavic: brat – brother, noc – night, woda – water. Polish nouns have seven cases; in English, word order does that job – Ola sees Tom is not the same as Tom sees Ola.
sprachen.cmp.franzoesisch: French is Romance, English is Germanic – both Indo-European. But after the Norman Conquest of 1066, English took thousands of words from French: table, beef, people, government. So you will recognise a lot.
sprachen.cmp.italienisch: Italian comes from Latin – and so do many English words, often through French: nation, family, important, possible. The short everyday words are mostly Germanic, though.
sprachen.cmp.spanisch: Spanish is Romance and distantly related to English: noche – night, tres – three. Many longer English words come from Latin, so they look familiar: hospital, animal, possible. Hermano and brother, though, have different roots.
sprachen.cmp.arabisch: Arabic belongs to the Afro-Asiatic family and is not related to English. But English has many words from Arabic, often through other languages: sugar (sukkar), coffee (qahwa), algebra (al-jabr), zero (ṣifr).
sprachen.cmp.tuerkisch: Turkish is a Turkic language and not related to English. Still, there are bridges: yoghurt and kiosk came into English through Turkish – and Turkish has taken words like futbol from English.
sprachen.cmp.chinesisch: Chinese is Sino-Tibetan and not related to English. Good news: English has no tones, and verbs hardly change – only the -s in she works. And the word tea came from the Hokkien Chinese word tê, through Dutch traders.
sprachen.cmp.vietnamesisch: Vietnamese is Austroasiatic and not related to English. But you already know the Latin alphabet – that makes reading and writing easier. And English has no tones.
sprachen.cmp.tagalog: Tagalog is Austronesian and not related to English – ina, gabi and bahay have completely different roots. But English is an official language in the Philippines, and Filipino has taken many English words.
sprachen.cmp.deutsch: German and English are siblings – both West Germanic. Many basic words are almost the same. The word decoder below explains why they still sound different.
sprachen.cmp.note: Being related helps with vocabulary – for grammar and pronunciation, practice is what counts.
sprachen.dec.title: German → English: the word decoder
sprachen.dec.lead: German and English are siblings: many words are really the same word. From around the 6th century German changed some sounds (the “High German consonant shift”); English kept the older ones. If you know German, these patterns help you guess English words.
sprachen.dec.step1: At the top is a sound swap: the German sound on the left, the English sound on the right.
sprachen.dec.step2: Below are examples: German word → English word.
sprachen.dec.step3: Try it with a German word you know: swap the sound back – often the English word comes out.
sprachen.dec.note: The first four patterns come from the consonant shift; the others are later changes. They're rules of thumb – not every word fits.
sprachen.dec.quiz: Try it yourself: what is it in English?

dialekte.title: Accents of English in the British Isles
dialekte.lead: From Scouse to Geordie: how English sounds in different parts of the UK and Ireland. Pick a region for examples and typical words, or see how people say hello and what they call a bread roll.
dialekte.map.title: The accent map
dialekte.map.lead: The colours show six big groups: the North of England, the Midlands, the South, Scotland, Wales and Ireland. The dots are well-known city accents and the Celtic languages.
dialekte.map.empty: Click a region or a dot on the map.
dialekte.map.wordNote: Simplified: in many places you hear several words, and the standard word is understood everywhere.
dialekte.group.north.text: Bus rhymes with push, and bath has a short a. Many words come from Old Norse.
dialekte.group.midlands.text: Between North and South: northern vowels (bus, bath), but a melody of its own.
dialekte.group.south.text: In much of the South bath has a long ah, and bus a short /ʌ/. Without an r in car – except in the West Country.
dialekte.group.scotland.text: The r is always pronounced. Many people also speak Scots, and some Scottish Gaelic.
dialekte.group.wales.text: English with a Welsh melody. Many people in the north and west speak Welsh first.
dialekte.group.ireland.text: The r is pronounced, th often sounds like t or d, and Irish shapes the grammar.
dialekte.r.northeast: Geordie is the accent of Tyneside; Mackem is the accent of Sunderland. Many words are old and close to Scots: bairn (child), gan (go), hyem (home). “Pet” and “hinny” are friendly ways to talk to someone.
dialekte.r.cumbria: Cumbrian English in the far north-west of England has many words from Old Norse, the language of the Vikings who settled here. Farmers in the Lake District once counted sheep with old numbers like yan, tyan, tethera.
dialekte.r.yorkshire: Yorkshire people are proud of their accent. Typical sounds: short a in bath and grass, bus rhymes with push, and the often becomes just t’ (“going t’ shop”). Hull has its own sound: “phone” can sound like “fern”.
dialekte.r.northwest: In Manchester people say “our kid” for a brother or sister and “dead good” for very good. Some older speakers in rural Lancashire still pronounce the r in car. Liverpool, at the western edge, has an accent of its own: Scouse (see the dot).
dialekte.r.westmidlands: The Black Country, west of Birmingham, keeps many old forms: “yow am” for you are – that is why people from there are nicknamed yam-yams. In the Potteries around Stoke-on-Trent, people call each other “duck”. Birmingham has its own dot: Brummie.
dialekte.r.eastmidlands: “Ey up, me duck” is the classic East Midlands greeting – “duck” is friendly, for anyone. Like in the North, bus rhymes with push and bath has a short a. Mardy (moody) is known all over England.
dialekte.r.eastanglia: In Norfolk you often hear “noo” for new and “Hoo” for Hugh: the y sound before u disappears. Verbs can drop the -s: “she like it”. The melody goes up and down a lot.
dialekte.r.southeast: Estuary English, between Cockney and standard southern English, has spread far beyond London: the t in “water” or “get it” becomes a stop in the throat, and l at the end of a word sounds like w (“miwk” for milk). This is close to the accent many textbooks use.
dialekte.r.southwest: The West Country is the only big part of England where many people still pronounce the r in car and farm. In Bristol, an l is often added at the end of words: “idea” can sound like “ideal”.
dialekte.r.lowlands: Here people speak Scottish English, and many also speak Scots, a sister language of English. The r is always pronounced, often rolled or tapped, and “loch” has the ch sound of German Bach. Glasgow has its own dot.
dialekte.r.northeastscotland: Doric is the Scots of Aberdeen and the North East. Its best-known feature: wh becomes f, so “fit” means what and “far” means where. “Fit like?” – “Nae bad” is a whole conversation.
dialekte.r.highlands: Highland English is often said to be soft and clear. Many families here once spoke Scottish Gaelic, and some still do, especially in the islands – so English here has a Gaelic melody and Gaelic words.
dialekte.r.northernisles: Until the 1700s many people here spoke Norn, a language close to Norwegian. The local Scots still has many Norse words, and Shetlanders say “du” to friends, like Norwegians. On the map, Shetland is shown in a box: it really lies further north.
dialekte.r.northmidwales: In the north and west of Wales, many people grow up speaking Welsh and learn English as a second language. Welsh English has the Welsh sing-song melody and some Welsh sentence patterns: “There’s lovely!”, “Coming tomorrow, is he?”
dialekte.r.southwales: Most people in the south speak English as their first language, but the Welsh melody stayed – “Wenglish”. “Now” does not always mean now: “I’ll do it now” can mean later. Cardiff’s own accent has a long, flat a: “Kairdiff”.
dialekte.r.ulster: Ulster English mixes Irish English with Scots, brought by settlers from Scotland in the 17th century. Statements often go up at the end, so they can sound like questions. Ulster Scots is spoken in parts of Antrim and Down. Belfast has its own dot.
dialekte.r.southirish: Irish English keeps patterns from Irish (Gaelic): “I’m after eating” means I have just eaten. The r is pronounced, and th often sounds like t or d: “tree” for three. Cork is known for its fast, sing-song accent.
dialekte.m.liverpool: Scouse sounds very different from the towns around it. A k or t can become a hissing sound in the throat: “back” sounds a bit like “bach”. The name comes from scouse, a stew of meat and potatoes.
dialekte.m.birmingham: Brummie has a falling melody that is easy to recognise, and “I” sounds close to “oy”. Birmingham is the UK’s second-largest city, and its accent is often heard on TV.
dialekte.m.london: Cockney is the old accent of the East End: “fink” for think, no h in “’ouse”, and rhyming slang. Today many young Londoners speak Multicultural London English (MLE), with words from Jamaican Patois, other languages and street slang.
dialekte.m.glasgow: Glaswegian is fast and full of Scots: “gonnae” (going to), “dinnae” (don’t), “wean” (child, from wee one). The t in the middle of a word often disappears into the throat: “wa’er” for water.
dialekte.m.belfast: In Belfast, “What about ye?” (often just “Bout ye?”) means hello. Belfast vowels sound very different from English accents, and many sentences go up at the end.
dialekte.m.dublin: Dublin English has its own words and a quick rhythm. Like everywhere in Ireland, people say “grand” for fine and use “ye” or “youse” for more than one person.
dialekte.m.welsh: Welsh (Cymraeg) is a Celtic language and an official language in Wales, next to English. Road signs and schools are bilingual, and in parts of the north and west most people speak Welsh at home.
dialekte.m.gaelic: Scottish Gaelic is a Celtic language, related to Irish. It is strongest in the Outer Hebrides; many place names all over the Highlands come from Gaelic.
dialekte.m.irish: Irish (Gaeilge) is the first official language of Ireland. Everyone learns it at school, but it is the everyday language mainly in the Gaeltacht, areas in the west such as Connemara.
dialekte.m.cornish: Cornish (Kernewek) is a Celtic language related to Welsh and Breton. It stopped being spoken as an everyday language in the 18th century; today a small community has brought it back.
dialekte.m.manx: Manx (Gaelg) is the Celtic language of the Isle of Man, which is not part of the UK. Its last native speaker died in 1974; today children can learn it again at a Manx-language primary school.
dialekte.lines.title: Two lines divide England
dialekte.lines.lead: Two sound changes happened in the south of England from about the 17th century and never reached the north. The lines on the map show roughly where they stop – they run close together from the Welsh border to the Wash.
dialekte.lines.benrath.title: The bus line: /bʊs/ | /bʌs/
dialekte.lines.benrath.text: North of the line, bus, cup and love have the same vowel as push and put (/ʊ/). South of it, they have a different vowel (/ʌ/), so putt and put sound different. Linguists call this the FOOT–STRUT split.
dialekte.lines.speyer.title: The bath line: short a | long ah
dialekte.lines.speyer.text: North of the line, bath, grass and laugh have the same short a as cat. South of it, in much of the south-east, they have a long ah (/ɑː/), as in father. Linguists call this the TRAP–BATH split.
dialekte.lines.note: Simplified: inside every group there are many local accents, and younger speakers often sound different from older ones. Most phonetic signs here are rough guides.
dialekte.learn.title: Do I have to learn an accent?
dialekte.learn.text: No. Standard English is understood everywhere, and you need it for exams, school and work. But it helps to recognise a few accents and words from the place where you live: “Alright?”, “Ey up” or “Hiya” open many doors. If you move to a region with a strong accent, listening to local speakers is the best practice.
dialekte.src.title: Sources
dialekte.src.text: A simplified overview based on J. C. Wells, Accents of English (1982), the British Library’s “Sounds Familiar?” collection and the Wikipedia articles on the accents and languages named here (checked November 2026). Real accent borders are fluid; the areas and lines are drawn roughly. Map outlines: Natural Earth (public domain).

satzmelodie.caveat: Careful, echo question ↗↗: “You're coming tomorrow?” is not a normal question. A yes/no question starts with a helping verb: “Are you coming tomorrow?” The echo question keeps the word order of a statement; only the voice goes up a lot. It also means something different: you're surprised or checking that you heard right (“Really? You're coming tomorrow?”). In writing and in exams, use the normal question.

satzmelodie.rule.title: The melody at the end of the sentence
satzmelodie.rule.aussage: The voice falls at the end.
satzmelodie.rule.w: The voice falls at the end, as in a statement. Questions with what, where, when, who, why, how and which.
satzmelodie.rule.jn: It starts with a helping verb (are, do, can, have …). The voice rises at the end.
satzmelodie.rule.echo: Word order like a statement, but the voice rises a lot. Not a normal question: you're surprised or checking. A yes/no question starts with a helping verb (“Are you from Poland?”).
satzmelodie.rule.ausruf: The stressed word goes very high, then the voice falls a long way. Feeling: joy, anger, surprise.
satzmelodie.rule.liste: The voice stays up → until the list is finished. Then it falls ↘.

wissen.lernen.lead: Mistakes are allowed. Even more: without mistakes you learn more slowly. Here Bruno, Regi, Hamsti and Quaki explain how your brain really holds on to English.
wissen.lernen.jungle.title: Your brain is a jungle
wissen.lernen.jungle.lead: Imagine this: a new word lies on the other side of a dense jungle. There's no path to it yet. You have to cut it yourself.
wissen.lernen.jungle.machete.title: The machete
wissen.lernen.jungle.machete.text: Learning is your machete. On your first try you hack your way through the jungle with effort. That's tiring – and completely normal.
wissen.lernen.jungle.falsch.title: The wrong way
wissen.lernen.jungle.falsch.text: Sometimes you walk in the wrong direction: a mistake. Your brain notices the difference between what it expected and the right answer. That very signal shows it where the path really goes.
wissen.lernen.jungle.pfad.title: The beaten path
wissen.lernen.jungle.pfad.text: Every time you walk the path again, it gets wider. Nerve cells that often work together connect more strongly.
wissen.lernen.jungle.strasse.title: The road
wissen.lernen.jungle.strasse.text: After many repetitions the path has become a road. You don't have to think anymore – the word is just there. Practice even changes the wiring in your brain along the way.
wissen.lernen.jungle.foot1: And a path you don't walk for a long time? It slowly grows over again. That's why you repeat (Rule 3).
wissen.lernen.jungle.foot2: Your brain constantly rebuilding itself like this is called neuroplasticity. Adults who learn to juggle for three months have measurably more grey matter afterwards
wissen.lernen.jungle.foot4: And London taxi drivers, who learn thousands of streets, have a changed hippocampus
wissen.lernen.jungle.foot5: Your brain learns at any age.
wissen.lernen.wheel.label: The seven rules
wissen.lernen.wheel.title: The learning circle
wissen.lernen.rule.fehler.title: Making mistakes is part of it
wissen.lernen.rule.fehler.text: You're not supposed to get everything right straight away. If you try an answer, get it wrong and then see the right one, you remember it better than if you only read it.
wissen.lernen.rule.fehler.why: A mistake surprises your brain. That surprise makes the correction stick. Even mistakes you were completely sure about get corrected especially well afterwards. The only important thing: always look at the right answer.
wissen.lernen.rule.erinnern.say: Hmm … what was it called again?
wissen.lernen.rule.erinnern.title: Recall first, then check
wissen.lernen.rule.erinnern.text: Reading a word list five times feels good – but doesn't do much. Better: cover the word and quiz yourself. Only then do you check.
wissen.lernen.rule.erinnern.why: Every time you pull a word out of your head, the path to it gets wider. Reading only goes through your eyes. Remembering is work, and that very work is what stays.
wissen.lernen.rule.oft.title: A little, but often – and sleep well
wissen.lernen.rule.oft.text: Ten minutes every day are better than two hours on Sunday. And when you've almost forgotten a word, that's the best moment to review it.
wissen.lernen.rule.oft.why: With breaks between reviews, knowledge stays much longer. While you sleep, your brain sorts what you learned during the day. So learning in the evening and a quick review in the morning go well together.
wissen.lernen.rule.mischen.title: Mix instead of blocks
wissen.lernen.rule.mischen.text: Twenty sentences with only the present perfect are easy – you already know what's coming. In real life you don't. So mix it up: past simple, present perfect, past continuous, all jumbled.
wissen.lernen.rule.mischen.why: When you mix, you learn not only the rule but also when you need it. That's harder, but it's exactly what you need in conversation and in the exam.
wissen.lernen.rule.laut.title: Speak out loud, don't just read
wissen.lernen.rule.laut.text: Read new sentences out loud. Speak along when you listen to audio. Even alone in the kitchen – that's not weird, that's training.
wissen.lernen.rule.laut.why: What you say out loud, you also hear, and you move your mouth while doing it. So your head remembers the sentence in several ways. And your mouth learns the words before you need them in a conversation.
wissen.lernen.rule.schwer.title: It can be hard – but not too hard
wissen.lernen.rule.schwer.text: If everything is easy, you learn little. If everything is too hard, you give up. You learn the most in between: you have to think, but you usually manage.
wissen.lernen.rule.schwer.why: The effort isn't a sign that you're bad at it. It's the sign that you're learning right now. Choose your level so that you get about eight out of ten tasks right.
wissen.lernen.rule.feiern.title: Celebrate small steps
wissen.lernen.rule.feiern.text: Don't compare yourself with others. Compare yourself with yourself a month ago. Every new word is a step.
wissen.lernen.rule.feiern.why: Anyone who sees their progress keeps learning. Small goals that you really reach keep you going longer than one big goal that's far away.
wissen.lernen.sum.title: In short
wissen.lernen.sum.1: Try it yourself first – even if you get it wrong.
wissen.lernen.sum.2: After every mistake, look at the right answer.
wissen.lernen.sum.3: Better a little every day than a lot once.
wissen.lernen.sum.4: Mix the topics and speak out loud.
wissen.lernen.studies.title: The studies
wissen.lernen.studies.lead: The asterisks (*) in the text lead here. The studies are in English.
wissen.lernen.study.schultz: The brain signals the difference between expectation and outcome – this error signal steers learning.
wissen.lernen.study.rumelhart: Artificial neural networks learn by correcting their connections a little after every error.
wissen.lernen.study.hebb: Nerve cells that are often active at the same time connect more strongly – the basic idea behind the “beaten path”.
wissen.lernen.study.bengtsson: A lot of practice changes the nerve pathways themselves (the white matter).
wissen.lernen.study.draganski: After three months of juggling, adults' grey matter grew – and shrank back when they stopped.
wissen.lernen.study.boyke: The same works for people around 60, too.
wissen.lernen.study.maguire: London taxi drivers, who learn thousands of streets, have a changed hippocampus – the longer in the job, the clearer it is.
wissen.lernen.study.kornell: Guessing wrong first and then seeing the answer helps more than reading the answer straight away.
wissen.lernen.study.butterfield: Mistakes you were sure about are remembered especially well after they are corrected.
wissen.lernen.study.metcalfe: Overview: mistakes that get corrected help learning instead of harming it.
wissen.lernen.study.roediger: Quizzing yourself keeps knowledge longer than reading it again.
wissen.lernen.study.cepeda: Reviewing with breaks in between beats learning in one go.
wissen.lernen.study.rasch: During sleep the brain consolidates what was learned during the day.
wissen.lernen.study.rohrer: Mixed tasks did clearly better in the later test than tasks in blocks.
wissen.lernen.study.macleod: Words read aloud are remembered better than words read silently.
wissen.lernen.study.bjork: “Desirable difficulties”: what feels hard while practising often stays longer.
wissen.lernen.study.wilson: Learning models make the fastest progress when they get about 85% of the tasks right.
